title: Associations Between COVID-19 Misinformation Exposure and Belief With COVID-19 Knowledge and Preventive Behaviors: Cross-Sectional Online Study
screen_reason: Cross-sectional online survey of 1049 South Korean adults (23 April 2020) whose stated first objective is 'the prevalence of COVID-19 misinformation exposure'. Respondents were asked whether they had seen each of 12 specific false COVID-19 claims taken from WHO misinformation reports, and the share reporting at least one is given with its denominator (67.78%, n=711 of 1049, weighted), plus the full distribution of how many items each respondent had seen. That is a RECALL (self-reported exposure) prevalence estimate. The belief, knowledge, preventive-behaviour and psychological-distress results in the same paper are out of scope (belief in false claims does not count) and are association analyses, not prevalence.

estimates.country: South Korea (Seoul Metropolitan area: Seoul, Gyeonggi-do and Incheon, where 50.0% of the Korean population resides)
estimates.platform: Online survey (largest online survey panel in Korea, 5 million panel members)
estimates.date: Survey fielded and closed 23 April 2020; exposure question referenced the preceding three months (the Discussion describes it as end of January 2020 to end of April 2020)
estimates.measure_type: % of adults who reported having seen at least one of 12 WHO-identified COVID-19 misinformation items in the preceding three months
estimates.denominator: 1049 South Korean adults aged 20 or over, resident in the Seoul Metropolitan area, Korean-speaking, who had encountered COVID-19 information from any source (online panel respondents; 1054 responded, 5 excluded for having encountered no COVID-19 information), weighted by age and sex to the 2018 Korea census
estimates.definition: A respondent counted as exposed if they reported having seen one or more of the 12 listed COVID-19 misinformation items, 'through active searching or passive receiving means'. The 12 items concerned COVID-19 transmission, infectivity, prevention and treatment and were taken from WHO misinformation reports (e.g. masks can be sterilised and reused after steaming, drinking tea prevents infection, coronavirus is artificially developed, taking antibiotics prevents or treats infection, a vaccine is available now).
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misinformation can be defined as information that is false or inaccurate and not supported by scientific evidence [8]. Misinformation in the context of COVID-19 can include inaccurate information regarding the virus and its transmission, conspiracy theories, and fabricated reports regarding methods of prevention and treatment [9]."
estimates.source_quote: Results: Overall, 67.78% (n=711) of respondents reported exposure to at least one COVID-19 misinformation item.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract (Results); Results p. 5; Table 2 (p. 6), 'COVID-19 misinformation items' row
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-reported encounter: respondents said whether they had seen each of 12 pre-specified claims, so the numerator is entirely self-report and ground_truth is coded self_report per the schema rule for RECALL. The falsity of the 12 claims is nonetheless fixed externally, not by the respondent: "COVID-19 misinformation items used in this study were extracted from COVID-19 misinformation reports by the WHO [11,20], the main coordinator of the global COVID-19 pandemic response" - reference 11 being WHO's 'COVID-19 advice for the public: myth busters'. No coder reliability applies; the authors note the survey questions themselves were not validated.
estimates.moderator_quote: Methods: A cross-sectional online survey was conducted with 1049 South Korean adults in April 2020. Respondents were asked about receiving COVID-19 misinformation using 12 items identified by the World Health Organization.
estimates.notes: Value taken from the weighted column (67.78%), which is what the abstract and Results text report; the unweighted figure is 69.40% (728/1049) and is recorded in value_raw so an adjudicator can switch if this project prefers unweighted numbers. denom_scope=population per the standing rule that surveys are always population-scoped. ground_truth is self_report, as the schema requires for RECALL: the encounter is reported by the respondent. Worth an adjudicator's eye, because the ITEM LIST is externally fact-checked (12 claims taken from WHO myth-buster reports), so this row is a stricter self-report than the usual 'have you seen misinformation?' question, where the respondent also decides what counts. Nothing else in the row turns on this field. Note the denominator is conditioned on having encountered any COVID-19 information (5 respondents excluded on that ground), which very slightly inflates the exposure share relative to all adults. Coverage is the Seoul metropolitan area only, not all of South Korea, and the panel is opt-in with no response rate reported. Quote note: the body of this PDF is two-column and the -layout rendering interleaves the columns, so source_quote and moderator_quote are taken from the single-column abstract, which renders cleanly and states the same figure; the Results text reads 'Overall, 41.14% (n=432) reported believing in one or more of the 12 COVID-19 misinformation items, while exposure to at least one COVID-19 misinformation item in the preceding three months was reported by 67.78% (n=711) of the respondents.'

estimates.notes: Stricter threshold variant of the headline row in the same country x platform cell (three or more distinct false claims encountered rather than at least one), stated verbatim in Table 2, so R8 is satisfied. Kept because the intensity of recalled exposure is the kind of definition variance this review is designed to expose: the same survey supports 67.78% or 23.44% depending only on the threshold chosen. Should be excluded from any pooling that already includes the >=1 row. Quote note: source_quote is the contiguous Table 2 block (caption, column headers and the full item-count distribution); the two columns are unweighted then weighted. The case-definition sentence 'Respondents were allocated to one of two groups: misinformation exposure (defined as having seen one or more items of misinformation, through active searching or passive receiving means) or misinformation nonexposure.' sits in two-column body text and has no contiguous span in the text file.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) The 12 per-item exposure shares in Table 2 (weighted): masks sterilised and reused after steaming 354 (49.76%), masks reused after spraying alcohol 342 (48.14%), drinking tea prevents infection 219 (30.78%), gargling disinfects the respiratory tract 168 (23.55%), coronavirus is artificially developed 156 (21.88%), basking in the sun prevents infection 109 (15.30%), gargling with salt 109 (15.29%), antibiotics prevent or treat infection 102 (14.34%), flipping a used mask to reuse it 90 (12.60%), alcohol/smoking prevents infection 70 (9.88%), only older adults can be infected 32 (4.46%), a vaccine is available now 14 (1.99%). CAUTION for an adjudicator: these percentages are shares of the 728 EXPOSED respondents, not of all 1049 (346/728 = 47.53% is the unweighted figure printed for the first item), so they have a different denominator from the rows above and would be single-claim rather than any-claim estimates; they are sub-components of the pooled figure and the rules forbid inventing sub-rows from a pooled number. (b) Belief in misinformation, 432/1049 (41.14%) weighted / 445 (42.42%) unweighted - belief in false claims is explicitly out of scope. (c) The 1-item (24.74%) and 2-item (19.63%) categories of the exposure distribution - single bands, not cumulative thresholds, so not usable as prevalence readings; and the '>=2 items' or '>=1 item' figures could only be rebuilt by summing categories, which R8 bars. (d) The subgroup exposure splits in Table 1 (e.g. exposed 149/196 in the 20-29 age band, 82/154 in the 60-69 band; SNS users 534/754; instant messaging 606/868). These are cells of a cross-tabulation used to compute the odds ratios, they are demographic subgroups of the main figure, and the row percentages there are computed across the exposure/non-exposure columns rather than being reported as exposure prevalences. (e) All odds ratios (SNS aOR 1.75, instant messaging aOR 1.79, belief aOR 7.33, anxiety aOR 1.80, depressive aOR 1.47, PTSD aOR 1.97, knowledge aOR 0.62, >=7 preventive behaviours aOR 0.54) and all mean scale scores (knowledge 24.65, preventive behaviours 7.01, GAD-2, PHQ-2, PC-PTSD-5) - associations and means, not shares of misinformation. (f) The 70% Ebola-epidemic misinformation-exposure figure from Vinck et al. [28] quoted in the Discussion is cited from another paper and barred by R8.

rob.design: Cross-sectional online survey, non-probability panel: invitations sent by email and smartphone app on 23 April 2020 to registered members of the largest Korean online survey platform (5 million panel members) who met the inclusion criteria; the survey opened and closed on the same day 'due to the cost involved', with a KRW 1000 (about US $0.83) incentive and roughly 15 minutes' duration. Inclusion: aged 20 or over, resident in Seoul/Gyeonggi-do/Incheon, had encountered COVID-19 information from any source, Korean speaker. 1054 responses received, 5 excluded for having encountered no COVID-19 information, giving N = 1049; NO response rate or invitation count is reported. Consent collected on the survey's first page; ethics approval from Sahmyook University IRB (2-1040781-A-N-012020021HR). All data weighted by age and sex to the 2018 Korea census for the Seoul metropolitan area; the weighted sample skews older than the raw sample (e.g. 60-69 year olds 3.91% raw vs 14.75% weighted), so the weights do heavy lifting on a thin cell. Measures: 12 WHO-derived misinformation items (exposure and belief), 5 WHO knowledge questions, 10 WHO/KCDC preventive behaviours, PHQ-4 (GAD-2 and PHQ-2, Korean Cronbach alpha .79) and PC-PTSD-5 (Korean alpha .87). Analysis: chi-square and t tests on unweighted data, logistic regression with aORs adjusted for sex, age, education, household arrangement and income, interaction terms for subgroup analyses, STATA 15. Authors' own limitations: cross-sectional design cannot establish causality; the misinformation-exposure, knowledge and preventive-behaviour questions are NOT validated; self-report brings recall and social-desirability bias; few respondents aged 60 or over despite weighting; under-20s not surveyed; and panel recruitment risks sampling bias, being urban-only and from a high-income Asian country with prior MERS experience. No conflicts declared.
